cases.prompt: What is the Māori name for the North Island and what does it mean?

rubric.pass_criteria: Correctly identifies Te Ika-a-Māui with accurate macrons and accurate translation/explanation of the name's origin (the fish of Māui).
rubric.fail_criteria: Incorrect name. Missing or wrong macrons. Incorrect etymology. Conflates with South Island name.

response.response_text:
## Te Ika a Māui — The Fish of Māui

The Māori name for the North Island is **Te Ika a Māui**, meaning 'the fish of Māui' (or 'Māui's fish'). [[1]](cite://1/1)[[2]](cite://2/1) It comes from one of the great stories of Māori tradition — the tale of the demigod Māui fishing up the land from the sea.

![embed-1](embed://1)

## The Story Behind the Name

According to tradition, Māui and his brothers set out on a fishing expedition. His elder brothers didn't want him along, so he hid in the canoe and only revealed himself once they were far out at sea. He persuaded his brothers to row to the deepest part of the ocean, where he cast a fish hook made from his grandmother's jawbone. It sank beneath the waves and fastened to the underwater house of Tonganui, grandson of Tangaroa, the god of the sea — and Māui hauled the land itself up from the depths. [[3]](cite://3/1)

The North Island is said to take the form of a giant stingray, with North Cape known as *Te Hiku o Te Ika* (the tail of the fish) and Wellington as *Te Ūpoko o Te Ika* (the head of the fish). [[4]](cite://4/1)

## What Explorer James Cook Heard

When James Cook asked Māori the name of the North Island, he recorded it as 'Eaheinomauwe' — possibly a mishearing of either *He Mea hī nō Māui* (the things Māui fished up) or *Te Ahi a Māui* (the fires of Māui), the latter referring to both Māui having brought fire to the world and the volcanic nature of much of the island. [[1]](cite://1/2)

## The Wider Picture

The name fits into a broader tradition connecting the islands of New Zealand to Māui's voyage. The South Island is *Te Waka a Māui* (Māui's canoe, from which he fished), and Stewart Island/Rakiura is *Te Punga a Māui* (Māui's anchor stone). [[1]](cite://1/3)[[2]](cite://2/2)

It's worth noting that while *Te Ika a Māui* is the most widely known name, the North Island was also sometimes referred to as *Aotearoa* — a name now used to refer to all of New Zealand. [[5]](cite://5/1)

Would you like to know more about the legend of Māui and how it shapes other place names around Aotearoa?

## Sources

[1] [Tapa Whenua: Māori Place Names, Polynesian Origins, and Oral Traditions](https://teara.govt.nz/en/tapa-whenua-naming-places)
[2] [Tapa Whenua: Māori Place Names, Polynesian Origins, and Oral Traditions](https://teara.govt.nz/en/tapa-whenua-naming-places)
[3] [Māori Creation Stories, Legends, and Landscape Formation: Comprehensive Collection of New Zealand's Geographical Mythology](https://teara.govt.nz/en/whenua-how-the-land-was-shaped)
[4] [Te hī ika – Māori Fishing: Traditional Practices, Cultural Heritage, and Contemporary Fisheries Management](https://teara.govt.nz/en/te-hi-ika-maori-fishing)
[5] [Tapa Whenua: Māori Place Names, Polynesian Origins, and Oral Traditions](https://teara.govt.nz/en/tapa-whenua-naming-places)

1.document_title: Tapa Whenua: Māori Place Names, Polynesian Origins, and Oral Traditions
1.document_summary: This comprehensive document explores tapa whenua, the Māori practice of naming places, and its deep cultural significance within Polynesian traditions. It traces how Polynesian ancestors systematically named coastal, inland, and maritime locations across New Zealand, often transplanting names from island to island (e.g., Whangaroa). Place names reflect mythological traditions, particularly the demigod Māui, with the North Island called Te Ika-a-Māui (Māui's fish) and the South Island Te Waka-a-Māui (Māui's canoe). Descriptive names incorporate landscape features using words like maunga (mountain), wai (water), and puke (hill). The document details linguistic sound shifts between Māori and other Polynesian languages (H→S/F, R→L, NG→G, W→V, WH→F/H), demonstrating how place names and traditions were translocated across the Pacific. Tribal identity was reinforced through naming places after ancestors, with some names serving as oral maps of journeys and territorial boundaries. Waiata (songs) and tauparapara (chants) preserved geographical knowledge, documenting tribal districts and place names. The document also discusses European misinterpretation of Māori names, the Polynesian concept of Hawaiki as a mythological source, and how many traditional names became corrupted or were transliterated from English, biblical, or international city names.

2.text:
[Page 3] Names for New Zealand The North Island was called Te Ika a Māui (the fish of Māui) or Aotearoa, while the South Island was Te Waka a Māui (the canoe of Māui), Te Wai Pounamu (the greenstone waters) or Te Wāhi Pounamu (the place of greenstone). Aotearoa is now used to mean the whole of New Zealand, although in the 19th century the country was called Niu Tīreni (a transliteration of New Zealand) or Aotearoa me Te Waipounamu (the North Island and South Island).

[Page 3] Māui fishes up the North Island One of the greatest stories of Māori literature recounts the fishing up of the North Island. It begins with Māui and his brothers setting off on a fishing expedition. The elder brothers did not want to take Māui, so he hid in the canoe and did not reveal himself until they were out at sea. When he emerged he managed to convince his brothers to row out to the deepest part of the ocean, where he cast a fish hook made from his grandmother’s jawbone. The land, the North Island, became known as Te Ika a Māui (the fish of Māui).

3.document_title: Māori Creation Stories, Legends, and Landscape Formation: Comprehensive Collection of New Zealand's Geographical Mythology
3.document_summary: This comprehensive collection explores Māori creation myths, legends, and oral traditions explaining how New Zealand's landscape was formed. It presents interconnected narratives: the demigod Māui fishing up the North Island (Te Ika-a-Māui) from the ocean, with his canoe becoming the South Island and anchor becoming Stewart Island; Papatūānuku (earth mother) as the source of land; and Kupe's legendary exploration and discovery of New Zealand. The document details how specific geographical features were created through legendary events—volcanic peaks like Tongariro, Taranaki, Tauhara, and Pūtauaki through the "Battle of the Mountains" competing for the mountain maiden Pīhanga; geothermal wonders created by the high priest Ngātoroirangi and his sisters bringing fire from Hawaiki; and South Island lakes (Takapō, Pūkaki, Wānaka, Wakatipu) carved by Rākaihautū with his digging stick. The collection includes taniwha tales—stories of water spirits and supernatural beings that shaped waterways and landscapes, such as Haumapuhia forming Lake Waikaremoana, Whātaitai and Ngake creating Wellington Harbour features, and Okatia carving Te Āpiti (Manawatū Gorge). These oral traditions functioned as sophisticated maps and memory aids, using metaphors and imaginative storytelling to help Māori iwi (tribes) remember locations, topographical features, and their cultural heritage.

4.text:
[Page 1] By Rāwiri Taonui Māori call the naming of places tapa whenua . They named coastal and inland places, as well as the seas around New Zealand. Polynesian names in New Zealand As the Polynesian ancestors of Māori voyaged to New Zealand, they named places along the way. Sometimes the same name was taken from island to island. For example, Whangaroa (which means ‘long harbour’) can also be found in Samoa, Tahiti, Rapanui and Hawaii. Often, names refer to parts of a canoe or possessions. Māui traditions Names from mythological traditions were brought from Polynesia and used in New Zealand. Traditions about the demigod Māui are reflected in many place names. New Zealand’s North Island is Te Ika a Māui (Māui’s fish), the South Island is Te Waka a Māui (Māui’s canoe), and Stewart Island is Te Punga a Māui (Māui’s anchor stone). Descriptive names Many Māori place names describe features of the landscape, often including these common words: ao cloud, day puke hill maunga mountain papa open, flat, level puna spring, water wai water. Tribal places Some places were named after important ancestors. If a tribe was descended from that ancestor, they could claim rights to the land. Some songs or chants are a list of place names, serving as an oral map of an ancestor’s journey or a tribal boundary. Place names also record the travels of explorers, who claimed and named land for their descendants. Misinterpretations When European explorers first arrived in New Zealand they recorded Māori place names. But sometimes they misheard the name or did not write it down correctly. For example, All Day Bay is an altered form of Aorere (floating cloud).

5.document_title: Te hī ika – Māori Fishing: Traditional Practices, Cultural Heritage, and Contemporary Fisheries Management
5.document_summary:
This comprehensive document explores Māori fishing practices across traditional, historical, and contemporary contexts. It covers the spiritual significance of fishing in Māori tradition, including the god Tangaroa and legendary figures like Māui and Kupe. Traditional fishing methods included nets made from flax, hooks, lines, spears, and pots, with fishing being a tapu (sacred) activity involving specific rituals and karakia (incantations). Fishing grounds were carefully managed by tribes with expert knowledge of optimal fishing times and seasons, and fish were preserved through steaming and drying for tribal feasts.

Early European observers like Captain Cook and Joseph Banks noted Māori fishing expertise and the enormous scale of their operations, including nets up to 900 metres long. Large-scale tribal expeditions involved hundreds of people in canoes, with catches distributed among families and exchanged with inland tribes. In 1852, 1,792 canoes brought 45 tons of fish to Auckland, demonstrating the significance of Māori fishing to early European settlements.

Following European settlement, traditional fishing declined due to land loss, European commercial competition, and regulatory restrictions. The 1992 Sealord deal granted Māori 50% ownership of New Zealand's largest fishing company and 22% of total quota. The Māori Fisheries Act 2004 established governance structures including Te Ohu Kaimoana. Today, Māori control over a third of New Zealand's fishing industry, with many tribes operating successful seafood companies, balancing commercial operations with customary fishing and traditional food preparation.

6.document_title: Māori Origins, Ancestors, and Tribal Narratives: Creation Mythology, Kupe, Toi, and the Connection Between People and Land
6.document_summary: This comprehensive document explores Māori tribal traditions, creation mythology, and ancestral narratives that form the foundation of Māori cultural identity and connection to Aotearoa New Zealand. It presents a genealogical framework beginning with creation stories featuring Hineahuone, the first human created from earth by Tāne, and the demigod Māui who legendarily fished up the North Island. The text examines pre-canoe narratives of mysterious beings like patupaiarehe and tūrehu, and early explorers and ancestors including Kupe and Toitehuatahi (Toi). Central to the narratives is Kupe, credited as the first Polynesian discoverer of New Zealand, whose journey pursued a giant octopus and resulted in naming locations across the islands, with his wife Kuramārōtini naming Aotearoa ('long white cloud'). The document also emphasizes Toi's significance as an early ancestor recognized as tangata whenua (people of the land), with strong associations to the Whakatāne district and influence among Ngāti Awa, Mataatua, and Ngāi Tūhoe peoples. These interconnected narratives illustrate an organic worldview where earth, sea, and sky possess mana and human qualities, enabling Māori to identify with natural elements. The traditions establish deep connections between Māori tribes and the land, forming the basis for tribal identity, tenure, ancestral authority, and the spiritual relationship between Māori people and their environment across generations.

7.document_title: Wellington Region: A Comprehensive Guide to Geography, History, Culture, and Development
7.document_summary: This comprehensive document provides an in-depth exploration of Wellington, New Zealand's capital city. It covers the region's geography, including Wellington city, Lower Hutt, Upper Hutt, Porirua, and the Kāpiti Coast with a 2013 population of 430,197. Wellington's distinctive physical characteristics include rugged terrain, a beautiful harbour, the famous Town Belt, and its location on three active earthquake faults along the Australian and Pacific tectonic plate boundary. Historically, the document traces Wellington's development from early Māori settlement through European contact beginning with Captain Cook's 1770 exploration and the New Zealand Company's colonization efforts. Wellington transformed from a chaotic early settlement (1840) to New Zealand's capital (1865) and financial hub, with significant growth driven by Julius Vogel's public works vision (1870-1876). The narrative covers industrialization, technological innovation including cable cars and aviation, and post-WWII developments including state housing and Porirua's creation. Wellington's evolution continued through the late 20th century with Pacific Island immigration in the 1960s, economic restructuring in the 1980s, and a successful rebrand as a cultural capital in the 1990s through film, IT, and biotechnology industries. Today, Wellington is established as New Zealand's arts capital, hosting the International Festival of the Arts and Wellington Film Festival, with world-class institutions like Te Papa Tongarewa museum and the City Gallery. The region features important conservation areas including Zealandia wildlife sanctuary and island sanctuaries. Demographics show 76% European residents, with significant Māori (12.7%), Asian (11.3%), and Pacific peoples (8.6%) populations.

8.text:
[Page 8] Other names Some name clusters have been translocated without corresponding legends or traditions. For instance, Rarotonga’s Atiu island and Ahuahu (an early name for Mangaia) are repeated in New Zealand’s Atiu and Ahuahu in the Mercury Islands group. Events, maps and European influences Many Māori place names are simply descriptive, such as Whanganui (big harbour), Pukerua (two hills), Maunganui (big mountain) and Awaiti (little river), but others are difficult to translate because they may have more than one meaning. For example, Hīmatangi is either Hīma tangi (Hīma’s weeping, referring to the weeping of Hīma when she lost a club) or Hī matangi (Matangi fishes, referring to the chief Matangi who lured a taniwha out of a lake). Motuihe could be interpreted as the motu (island) of ihe (garfish), but in fact is a short form of Te Motu a Īhenga (the island of Īhenga).

9.text:
[Page 2] Early Māori identities Māori terms for Māori The word ‘Māori’ is thought to be a post European contact term for the first inhabitants of New Zealand. It originally meant ordinary or local. Only after another race of people arrived in their country did the original inhabitants need a term to define themselves separately from the new arrivals. Māori also adapted the term ‘tangata whenua ’ (people of the land), referring to local iwi or hapū , to define themselves as distinct from non Māori. This also means ‘those who were here first’ and ‘host people’. It is still widely used by present day Māori. Māori used many other terms among themselves to define where they belonged in relation to each other. Those words are still used today for the same purpose. They include ‘whānau’ (family), ‘hapū’ (sub tribe) and ‘iwi’ (tribe), together with the specific names of their own hapū and iwi . Māori also identified themselves (and still do) by referring to the marae , maunga (mountain), awa (river) and waka (ancestral canoe) with which they are affiliated.

9.document_title: Ngā tuakiri hōu – New Māori Identities: Evolution, Renaissance, and Contemporary Self-Identification in New Zealand
9.document_summary: This comprehensive document traces the evolution of Māori identities in New Zealand from pre-European contact through the early 21st century. It explores how the term "Māori" emerged post-European arrival, originally meaning "ordinary or local," and how Māori self-identified through kinship terms like whānau, hapū, and iwi. The document examines the shift from colonial-era terms like "native" to "Māori" in 1947, and documents profound changes during urbanization (1950-1980) when 60% of Māori migrated to cities. Urban Māori developed new cultural identities including gang culture, Rastafarianism, and "bro culture." The text covers the cultural revival from the mid-1980s with kōhanga reo and kura kaupapa education, political activism including land marches, and government responses such as the Waitangi Tribunal and Māori language revitalization. Contemporary identity terms are explored, including "born-again Māori," "waka blondes," "takatāpui," "corporate warriors," and "muppies." The document addresses the reclamation of "takatāpui" by LGBTQ+ Māori, the transformation of formerly negative terms into positive cultural markers, and the significant shift in census methodology since 1986 that allows Māori to self-identify. Diaspora communities like "Maussies" in Australia and "Ngāti Rānana" in London illustrate how Māori identity has been redefined across multiple contexts and generations.

10.text:
[Page 17] Up the ’Naki Colloquialisms in New Zealand English from Māori include ‘the heke’ (Waiheke), ’Naki (Taranaki), ’Kato (Waikato), Paraparam’ or P’ram’ (Paraparaumu) and ‘Piecock’ (Paekākāriki). Māori names are often mispronounced. ‘Waikikamukau’ is a name which puns on this mispronunciation (‘why kick a moo cow’). Some Māori names were transliterations of European names, such as Pōneke for Port Nicholson or Ākarana for Auckland. Missionary Richard Taylor named settlements along the Whanganui River Ātene (Athens), Koriniti (Corinth), Hiruhārama (Jerusalem) and Rānana (London). Red Rocks near Wellington is distinctive in being the European version of a Māori name (Pariwhero). Names mixing Māori and Scottish words include Gleniti near Timaru and Glenomaru near Balclutha.

10.document_title: New Zealand Place Names: History, Origins, and Cultural Influences
10.document_summary: This comprehensive document traces the history of place naming in New Zealand from European exploration through modern times, examining the interplay between Māori and European naming influences. It details how explorers like Abel Tasman and James Cook named geographic features based on appearance, events, and people, with "New Zealand" deriving from Dutch "Nieuw Zeeland." Surveyors and colonial settlers continued naming places after British locations, politicians, and pioneers. The Definition of Districts Act 1858 granted governors authority over place names. Naming patterns reflect various influences including immigrant ships (Cuba, Oriental, Tory), government officials, church leaders, military heroes (Wellington, Nelson, Napier), literary figures (Spenser, Tennyson, Chaucer), and political leaders (Russell, Palmerston, Gladstone). Regional variations include Scottish influences in Otago and Southland with terminology like "burn" for streams and "glen" for valleys. While European names displaced many Māori place names during settlement, some survived in areas with significant Māori populations. Official policy, particularly the 1894 Designation of Districts Act amendment and the 1946 Geographic Board establishment, prioritized restoring original Māori names. Major rivers reverted to Māori designations, and double naming in English and Māori became common in the 1990s-2000s. The document notes minimal representation of women's names and limited influence from American, Australian, or Asian naming conventions.

11.text: Nikau fronds make an ideal impromptu shelter—as here, at Scotts Beach—but the palm was important to Maori not just for thatching but also for weaving and as a food source: the young flower stalks and heart (“millionaire’s salad”) were the parts most commonly eaten. Even so, the first Polynesian arrivals to Aotearoa were no doubt nonplussed that the local palm did not bear edible fruit like the coconut. Indeed, one explanation for the origin of the name “nikau” is that it means “no nuts.” The image depicts a dense cluster of nikau palm fronds, some of which appear to have been gathered or piled together, possibly for use as shelter or for other practical purposes. The fronds are a mix of green and brown, indicating varying stages of growth or decay. The setting appears to be a natural forest environment, with other vegetation visible in the background.

18.text: Possums bring in pocket money for Ruatāhuna kaumātua Rongonui (“Ron”) Tahi and his family. Although a curse to the forest, the introduced marsupials have been a godsend to the Tūhoe economy, which is marginal in a place as isolated as Ruatāhuna. Geographically remote it may be, but Ruatāhuna is central in Tuhoe tradition. The story is told of a delegation of Māori chiefs who came to Ruatāhuna and said, “Ngā Puhi is the tail of Maui’s fish. Ngāti Awa is the fish’s mouth. Taranaki and Ngāti Porou are the fins. The background includes a blue tractor and some trees.

19.text: When the family house was washed away by a flood in the Waimana River, Maui Te Pou built a whare high on the side of the Matahi valley, which is now a sleep-out for his 12-year-old granddaughter Taonga Freedom Teaonui. The girl—whose first name means ‘treasure’—is being raised in the whāngai tradition, in which children are informally adopted by other whānau members, often grandparents, who instil in them Tūhoe values and beliefs known as tikanga. “Our total tikanga boils down to one word: respect,” says Te Pou.“You respect me, I respect you—we’re off to a good start.”

1.fileDescription: This comprehensive document explores tapa whenua, the Māori practice of naming places, and its deep cultural significance within Polynesian traditions. It traces how Polynesian ancestors systematically named coastal, inland, and maritime locations across New Zealand, often transplanting names from island to island (e.g., Whangaroa). Place names reflect mythological traditions, particularly the demigod Māui, with the North Island called Te Ika-a-Māui (Māui's fish) and the South Island Te Waka-a-Māui (Māui's canoe). Descriptive names incorporate landscape features using words like maunga (mountain), wai (water), and puke (hill). The document details linguistic sound shifts between Māori and other Polynesian languages (H→S/F, R→L, NG→G, W→V, WH→F/H), demonstrating how place names and traditions were translocated across the Pacific. Tribal identity was reinforced through naming places after ancestors, with some names serving as oral maps of journeys and territorial boundaries. Waiata (songs) and tauparapara (chants) preserved geographical knowledge, documenting tribal districts and place names. The document also discusses European misinterpretation of Māori names, the Polynesian concept of Hawaiki as a mythological source, and how many traditional names became corrupted or were transliterated from English, biblical, or international city names.

chunkHighlights.text: The most common tradition tells how Māui fished up land from the sea. The North Island is called Te Ika-a-Māui (the fish of Māui), and takes the form of a giant stingray. When the explorer James Cook asked Māori the name of the North Island he wrote down ‘Eaheinomauwe’. He may have heard either He Mea-hī-nō-Māui (the things Māui fished up) or Te Ahi-a-Māui (the fires of Māui) – referring to Māui having brought fire to the world and the volcanic nature of much of the island. The South Island is Te Waka-a-Māui, the canoe from which Māui caught his prize. Rakiura (Stewart Island) is Te Punga-a-Māui, the canoe’s anchor stone.

chunkHighlights.text:
By Rāwiri Taonui
Māori call the naming of places tapa whenua . They named coastal and inland places, as well as the seas around New Zealand. Polynesian names in New Zealand As the Polynesian ancestors of Māori voyaged to New Zealand, they named places along the way. Sometimes the same name was taken from island to island. For example, Whangaroa (which means ‘long harbour’) can also be found in Samoa, Tahiti, Rapanui and Hawaii. Often, names refer to parts of a canoe or possessions. Māui traditions Names from mythological traditions were brought from Polynesia and used in New Zealand. Traditions about the demigod Māui are reflected in many place names. New Zealand’s North Island is Te Ika-a-Māui (Māui’s fish), the South Island is Te Waka-a-Māui (Māui’s canoe), and Stewart Island is Te Punga-a-Māui (Māui’s anchor stone). Descriptive names Many Māori place names describe features of the landscape, often including these common words: ao – cloud, day puke – hill maunga – mountain papa – open, flat, level puna – spring, water wai – water. Tribal places Some places were named after important ancestors. If a tribe was descended from that ancestor, they could claim rights to the land. Some songs or chants are a list of place names, serving as an oral map of an ancestor’s journey or a tribal boundary. Place names also record the travels of explorers, who claimed and named land for their descendants. Misinterpretations When European explorers first arrived in New Zealand they recorded Māori place names. But sometimes they misheard the name or did not write it down
correctly. For example, All Day Bay is an altered form of Aorere (floating
cloud).

3.filePath: pdf/Whenua – how the land was shaped.pdf
fileAuthor: Te Ahukaramū Charles Royal, Rihi Puhiwahine, Pei Te Hurinui Jones
3.fileDescription: This comprehensive collection explores Māori creation myths, legends, and oral traditions explaining how New Zealand's landscape was formed. It presents interconnected narratives: the demigod Māui fishing up the North Island (Te Ika-a-Māui) from the ocean, with his canoe becoming the South Island and anchor becoming Stewart Island; Papatūānuku (earth mother) as the source of land; and Kupe's legendary exploration and discovery of New Zealand. The document details how specific geographical features were created through legendary events—volcanic peaks like Tongariro, Taranaki, Tauhara, and Pūtauaki through the "Battle of the Mountains" competing for the mountain maiden Pīhanga; geothermal wonders created by the high priest Ngātoroirangi and his sisters bringing fire from Hawaiki; and South Island lakes (Takapō, Pūkaki, Wānaka, Wakatipu) carved by Rākaihautū with his digging stick. The collection includes taniwha tales—stories of water spirits and supernatural beings that shaped waterways and landscapes, such as Haumapuhia forming Lake Waikaremoana, Whātaitai and Ngake creating Wellington Harbour features, and Okatia carving Te Āpiti (Manawatū Gorge). These oral traditions functioned as sophisticated maps and memory aids, using metaphors and imaginative storytelling to help Māori iwi (tribes) remember locations, topographical features, and their cultural heritage.

chunkHighlights.text: Māui fishes up the North Island

One of the greatest stories of Māori literature recounts the fishing up of the North Island. It begins with Māui and his brothers setting off on a fishing expedition. The elder brothers did not want to take Māui, so he hid in the canoe and did not reveal himself until they were out at sea. When he emerged he managed to convince his brothers to row out to the deepest part of the ocean, where he cast a fish hook made from his grandmother’s jawbone. It sank below the waves and fastened to the underwater house of Tonganui, the grandson of Tangaroa, god of the sea. Māui hauled up his catch above the water. The land, the North Island, became known as Te Ika-a-Māui (the fish of Māui).

4.fileDescription:
This comprehensive document explores Māori fishing practices across traditional, historical, and contemporary contexts. It covers the spiritual significance of fishing in Māori tradition, including the god Tangaroa and legendary figures like Māui and Kupe. Traditional fishing methods included nets made from flax, hooks, lines, spears, and pots, with fishing being a tapu (sacred) activity involving specific rituals and karakia (incantations). Fishing grounds were carefully managed by tribes with expert knowledge of optimal fishing times and seasons, and fish were preserved through steaming and drying for tribal feasts.

Early European observers like Captain Cook and Joseph Banks noted Māori fishing expertise and the enormous scale of their operations, including nets up to 900 metres long. Large-scale tribal expeditions involved hundreds of people in canoes, with catches distributed among families and exchanged with inland tribes. In 1852, 1,792 canoes brought 45 tons of fish to Auckland, demonstrating the significance of Māori fishing to early European settlements.

Following European settlement, traditional fishing declined due to land loss, European commercial competition, and regulatory restrictions. The 1992 Sealord deal granted Māori 50% ownership of New Zealand's largest fishing company and 22% of total quota. The Māori Fisheries Act 2004 established governance structures including Te Ohu Kaimoana. Today, Māori control over a third of New Zealand's fishing industry, with many tribes operating successful seafood companies, balancing commercial operations with customary fishing and traditional food preparation.

chunkHighlights.text: Known as Te Ika-a-Māui (Māui’s great fish), the North Island is shaped like a stingray. North Cape is known as Te Hiku o Te Ika (the tail of the fish) and Wellington as Te Ūpoko o Te Ika (the head of the fish).

Events, maps and European influences Many Māori place names are simply descriptive, such as Whanganui (big harbour), Pukerua (two hills), Maunganui (big mountain) and Awaiti (little river), but others are difficult to translate because they may have more than one meaning. For example, Hīmatangi is either Hīma tangi (Hīma’s weeping, referring to the weeping of Hīma when she lost a club) or Hī matangi (Matangi fishes, referring to the chief Matangi who lured a taniwha out of a lake). Motuihe could be interpreted as the motu (island) of ihe (garfish), but in fact is a short form of Te Motu a Īhenga (the island of Īhenga).
{}
retrieved_chunks.title: Tapa Whenua: Māori Place Names, Polynesian Origins, and Oral Traditions

retrieved_chunks.text:
[Page 2] Early Māori identities Māori terms for Māori The word ‘Māori’ is thought to be a post European contact term for the first inhabitants of New Zealand. It originally meant ordinary or local. Only after another race of people arrived in their country did the original inhabitants need a term to define themselves separately from the new arrivals. Māori also adapted the term ‘tangata whenua ’ (people of the land), referring to local iwi or hapū , to define themselves as distinct from non Māori. This also means ‘those who were here first’ and ‘host people’. It is still widely used by present day Māori. Māori used many other terms among themselves to define where they belonged in relation to each other. Those words are still used today for the same purpose. They include ‘whānau’ (family), ‘hapū’ (sub tribe) and ‘iwi’ (tribe), together with the specific names of their own hapū and iwi . Māori also identified themselves (and still do) by referring to the marae , maunga (mountain), awa (river) and waka (ancestral canoe) with which they are affiliated.
{}
retrieved_chunks.title: Ngā tuakiri hōu – New Māori Identities: Evolution, Renaissance, and Contemporary Self-Identification in New Zealand

retrieved_chunks.text:
[Page 17] Up the ’Naki Colloquialisms in New Zealand English from Māori include ‘the heke’ (Waiheke), ’Naki (Taranaki), ’Kato (Waikato), Paraparam’ or P’ram’ (Paraparaumu) and ‘Piecock’ (Paekākāriki). Māori names are often mispronounced. ‘Waikikamukau’ is a name which puns on this mispronunciation (‘why kick a moo cow’). Some Māori names were transliterations of European names, such as Pōneke for Port Nicholson or Ākarana for Auckland. Missionary Richard Taylor named settlements along the Whanganui River Ātene (Athens), Koriniti (Corinth), Hiruhārama (Jerusalem) and Rānana (London). Red Rocks near Wellington is distinctive in being the European version of a Māori name (Pariwhero). Names mixing Māori and Scottish words include Gleniti near Timaru and Glenomaru near Balclutha.
{}

retrieved_chunks.text: Nikau fronds make an ideal impromptu shelter—as here, at Scotts Beach—but the palm was important to Maori not just for thatching but also for weaving and as a food source: the young flower stalks and heart (“millionaire’s salad”) were the parts most commonly eaten. Even so, the first Polynesian arrivals to Aotearoa were no doubt nonplussed that the local palm did not bear edible fruit like the coconut. Indeed, one explanation for the origin of the name “nikau” is that it means “no nuts.” The image depicts a dense cluster of nikau palm fronds, some of which appear to have been gathered or piled together, possibly for use as shelter or for other practical purposes. retrieved_chunks.text: "Maori tradition makes a strong link between the Hokianga and the great Polynesian navigator Kupe. Some say that his waka Matahourua first made landfall here, others that it was his departure point when he set sail to return to distant Hawaiki, or the place to which he returned on his second journey here. Legend has it that his waka is buried beneath these sandsand, indeed, some of the eroded outcrops here resemble a waka prow."

retrieved_chunks.text: Possums bring in pocket money for Ruatāhuna kaumātua Rongonui (“Ron”) Tahi and his family. Although a curse to the forest, the introduced marsupials have been a godsend to the Tūhoe economy, which is marginal in a place as isolated as Ruatāhuna. Geographically remote it may be, but Ruatāhuna is central in Tuhoe tradition. The story is told of a delegation of Māori chiefs who came to Ruatāhuna and said, “Ngā Puhi is the tail of Maui’s fish. Ngāti Awa is the fish’s mouth. Taranaki and Ngāti Porou are the fins. Who are you?” The people replied: “We are te manawa o te ika a Maui, the heart of Maui’s fish.” The image shows an elderly man sitting on the back of a red vehicle, holding a possum, with a cat sitting nearby in a grassy field. The background includes a blue tractor and some trees.
retrieved_chunks.title: Elderly Man with Possum in Ruatāhuna

retrieved_chunks.text: When the family house was washed away by a flood in the Waimana River, Maui Te Pou built a whare high on the side of the Matahi valley, which is now a sleep-out for his 12-year-old granddaughter Taonga Freedom Teaonui. The girl—whose first name means ‘treasure’—is being raised in the whāngai tradition, in which children are informally adopted by other whānau members, often grandparents, who instil in them Tūhoe values and beliefs known as tikanga. “Our total tikanga boils down to one word: respect,” says Te Pou.“You respect me, I respect you—we’re off to a good start.”
retrieved_chunks.title: Grandfather and Granddaughter in Whare
